"Of course you are," the man said, without a flicker, and the twenty slid back into his pocket like the end of a card trick. The phone went back up. It was so smooth it took Cal a second to feel it, and it was worse than the mistake. The mistake had at least been about him.

Cal took the twenty, carried the box, and on his way back out said "Thank you, sir" with a smile so polite you could have served it at a funeral. On the top step somebody laughed out loud and turned it into a cough.

They were friends in eight seconds, which Cal resented a little, the way you resent a song for being so sure of itself.

Cal touched it. "Bar fight. I won. Wicked narrowly."
From the stairwell below came the voice from the phone. "Bear, the rug."
Teddy's shoulders came down half an inch. "Coming!" he called, in a voice that wasn't the one he'd been using. Cal filed it.

Teddy's half of the room looked like a catalog mailed to the wrong house: a Ralph Lauren duvet, a PowerBook, a silver mini stereo, a framed photo of Teddy and his father in a racing shell with the father's hand on the back of Teddy's neck, and a lacrosse stick with the tags still on.
"You play?"
"God, no. My mother thinks it's a conversation starter."

Cal's half took four minutes. A Sox pennant. A photo of the twins at Castle Island, Siobhan holding her Sully's cone like evidence and Patrick with his whole face in his, both twelve, both squinting at Cal behind the camera. And the crucifix Patty had pressed on him last night in a Quiet Man bar towel. There was already a nail over the bed. He hung it without thinking, then turned around, and Teddy was looking at it.
So it was up now. Taking it down would need a sentence, and he didn't have one.
"That's nice," Teddy said. "No, genuinely." Then he went back to his stereo and kept not mentioning it so carefully and so kindly that Cal almost wished he'd made a joke. You could hit a joke back.
In the common room the TV was on CNN, a Category 3 grinding across the Gulf under its cone, until a boy in a popped collar said "Dude, no," and put on MTV.

On the stairs Cal met a mini-fridge coming up between a slight kid in wire glasses, a notebook in his back pocket, and a man in his sixties in a Hollis-green groundskeeper's shirt who had most of the weight. Cal took a corner. At the third-floor window they stopped to breathe. The town, the mill, the river flat and white in the haze.
"The river's that way," the kid said, to nobody. "They fenced the dam two weeks ago. A girl drowned."
"Henry," his father said.

Henry stopped. His father's hands stayed flat on the fridge. Then Henry pointed, as if to put something else in the window: a dark granite cube with no windows at all, out on the bluff at the end of the road.

His father almost smiled. "Up," he said, and they went.

A girl in pearls and a ribbon held the door, beside a woman in a hat the size of a patio umbrella. "If I may," she called down to the blonde, pure Charleston, "you must be my roommate, or else the bravest girl in Massachusetts. Do come in out of this heat before Mama offers you sweet tea and a husband." She came two steps down to take the other handle and was refused with the same smile as the boy, which seemed to delight her.
The blonde got the trunk onto the top step alone, looked straight across the lawn at Cal, and raised one eyebrow. Then she was inside.
Rich girl, Cal thought. Too rich to need parents. At the ID table the woman told him not to smile, and he did anyway.

He stood with his back to the window and the river and did the rules like a set at a club where somebody might get stabbed.

"Quiet hours begin at eleven on weeknights. Some of you have never heard of a weeknight. You'll learn. The fire doors are alarmed, by which I mean wired, not upset. If you're going to vomit, vomit in your own room; I'm an RA, not a priest." The laugh came and he didn't wait for it. "Anything else you'll regret, do it quietly and off this floor. Rules I enforce. Advice I watch."
He never smiled. The room loved him anyway.
Afterward he put two fingers on Cal's sleeve. "You're the Haverford Scholar. Don't look surprised; one reads the files."
"I wasn't looking surprised."
"You were looking at my suit. Same thing. You're my second."
"Second what?"

"Haverford Scholar. The first is giving the welcome at Convocation in an hour. Watch him; he's what this place does to people like you when it likes them." Down the hall Teddy was explaining to a boy from 302 why he didn't play lacrosse. "Your roommate will tell you tonight is about fraternities. Frats are for men who need a roof to feel important. Real power is behind a door on Prospect Street tonight, and you won't get through it. Presumably you've noticed the shoes."

Founders' Chapel was white clapboard under a white steeple, its square bell tower raised over the Commons like a hand at a meeting. Everyone already called it the Beacon. Inside it was hot as a laundromat. President Pyne spoke for eleven minutes about stewardship, and Cal suspected President Pyne wouldn't remember it either. Dean Carrow sat on the dais in a green bow tie, silver-haired, turning a gold signet ring as if he were winding something.

Then the Student Assembly President stood up. OWEN M. TIERNEY '06, said the program. His first joke got the balcony and his second got the parents, and under four years of polish, sanded nearly flat, was Dorchester. Cal heard it the way you'd hear a Sox score through a wall.

"My mother cleaned houses in Milton," Owen said. "Big ones, with libraries nobody read in. If I can be standing here, in a suit I'm still paying off, then believe me, you belong in this room." He waited past the laugh so they'd lean in. "So work hard, be good to the people who clean up after you, and when you look back on this year, I hope you can say what the old song says. 'Of all the harm that e'er I've done, alas it was to none but me.'" A grin. "Mostly."
The chapel laughed. Cal laughed, his heart going, because it was the first time all day anybody at Hollis had sounded like home.

body.text: Main Street ran downhill to the dead mill, and Canal Street peeled off it along the race, a stone channel where somebody had put the Calder to work in 1840 and the river was still sore about it. Cal followed the water past a laundromat and a packie with a hand-lettered sign that said WE CARD HOLLIES, until the street gave out at a brick counting house with a green door and a dead Narragansett sign in the window, the neon long since gone to glass.

Inside it was dark and cool and smelled like every bar he'd been parked in as a kid with a Shirley Temple and a coloring book. Tin ceiling. A mahogany bar that went back forty feet, so long and so rubbed it looked poured. In the middle of the floor was a square of thick glass, scuffed to fog at the corners, and under it the race went roaring past in the dark, two feet below the boots of an old man reading the *Gazette*. Nobody looked down. Cal stood on the glass anyway and felt it in his shins.

Behind the register the Sox had a shrine: Yaz, Fisk, a 2004 pennant with FINALLY across it in black marker, the letters pressed so hard they'd torn the felt. A jar of pickled eggs sat at the end of the bar, cloudy as a specimen. Nobody had opened it since Carter. On the TV in the corner NESN had the Sox, the grass that impossible green under the lights, and during the pitching change somebody had the sense to cut to the weather: a white cone laid over the Gulf of Mexico like a finger.
"That's going into New Orleans," said a man in a Carhartt vest, to no one. "Watch."
Nobody watched. "Put the game back," said a man at the end of the bar, and the game came back, and somebody fed the jukebox a quarter.
The bartender was fifty, with reading glasses pushed up into hair the color of a new penny and a Dunkin' cup that didn't have coffee in it. "You lost, hon?"
"I'm looking for the owner. Somebody told me he needs a barback."
"Somebody."
"Somebody." Julian had said *tell him*. Cal figured that meant him.

She looked at his hands before she looked at his face, which was how he knew she'd worked a long time. "Augie doesn't come down Saturdays till ten. Come back tomorrow before four. He'll want to look at you."
"Bonnie," she added, like a receipt, and went back to cutting limes.

By the hall to the bathrooms there was a wall of frames, forty or fifty, old bar tabs gone the color of tea behind glass, each with a name and a class year in somebody's square capitals. Bonnie saw him looking. "Wall of Shame. Hollis boys who walked out on a bill and went on to be somebody. Augie won't let them pay. He likes them owing."
R. ASHFORD '74 — $9.25 + ONE WINDOW. Cal liked R. Ashford already. N. SLOANE '87 — $46.50. And at eye level, in a better frame than the rest, T. VANDERHOEF '80 — $212.00.

He laughed out loud, a real one, loud enough that the *Gazette* came down an inch. Two hundred and twelve dollars was what he had in his sock, to the dollar, forty of it Patty's. Twenty-five years Teddy's old man had owed exactly what Cal owned in the world.
"What's funny?"
"I think I'm rooming with his kid."

Beside the register, under the Sox, was a graduation picture: a dark-haired girl with freckles and a gap in her front teeth, mortarboard crooked, laughing with her whole face like someone had just said the worst possible thing at the best possible moment. Under it sat a pickle jar with masking tape on the glass. FOR JO. Ones, mostly, and a Mass card.
"Who's Jo?"
"Augie's granddaughter."
"What happened?"
"She went swimming." Bonnie's face kept going for a second after her mouth stopped, the way a drawer slides after you let go of it, and then it shut.

then.text: Cal felt Theodore Vanderhoef III's twenty in his front pocket, where it had been riding all day like a splinter. He took it out, unfolded it so Jackson faced front, and put it in the jar. Bonnie watched him do it. She didn't say thank you, and he liked her for that.

"I'll be here," Cal said, which was.

body.text: Teddy was on his third shirt. The blue oxford lay across the desk chair like a man who'd fainted, the pink one was balled on the bed, and the white one was half buttoned while Teddy stood in front of the closet mirror in his boxers and dress socks with a hairbrush in his fist, singing.

He didn't stop when Cal came in. He pointed the hairbrush at him and took the chorus up and over, eyes shut, fully committed, and the thing was he was good, the kind of good that would have gotten him jumped at Cal's high school and cast as the lead at his. He hit the high part clean and held it and came down laughing.
"Don't tell anyone," Teddy said. "I have a reputation for being tone-deaf and I worked very hard for it."
"I'm going to need you to do that at my funeral."

"Booked." Teddy picked a tie off the bed, navy with a thin white stripe, and looped it on, and it came out fat and short and crooked, like a tongue. "Every Vanderhoef since McKinley has worn this tie, and every one of them has had a man to tie it."
"C'mere."

Cal had learned knots at seven for his First Communion and kept in practice with wakes, which in Southie came around more often. He turned Teddy by the shoulders and did it from behind, the way his grandfather had done his, a plain four-in-hand, the dimple pinched in with a thumb. Teddy held very still and looked at the two of them in the mirror.
"Nobody's done that since my grandfather," he said.
The Razr buzzed on the desk. The little outside screen said DAD. Teddy turned off the music before he answered, which told Cal most of what he needed.

"Hi, Dad." A voice came through the phone, not the words, just the shape, and then one word clear as a bell: *Bear*. Teddy's shoulders came in half an inch. His sentences got long and careful and buttoned, a father's sentences in a son's mouth. "Yes, sir. I'm dressing now. The navy. Yes. I'll give them your best. I will. Mom too." He closed the phone and sat on the bed and looked at it.
Then he looked up and he was Teddy again, like a light coming back on.
"Okay. New game. Say you were me. Hypothetically. A man with a face like a canned ham comes at you at a party and asks after your mother."
"How's your mother?"

"Bunny. Her hip. It's titanium now, and furious about it. Say that. 'Titanium and furious.' They love it. Next: the dog. Commodore. Black Lab, eleven, has never once been wrong about a person." He counted on his fingers, which was Cal's move. "We belong to the Round Hill Club. You never say Greenwich, Connecticut. You say Greenwich. If they need the state, they aren't worth talking to. And 'the city' is New York. Always. If you mean Boston, you're dead."
"What do I say about Boston?"
"You say 'Boston' like it's a nice girl you never called back."
Cal did it. "Oh, *Boston*," in Teddy's voice, with Teddy's little laugh coming a half-second early, and Teddy put both hands over his face.
"That's horrifying. Do it again."

The Razr went off a second time. LIBBY. Teddy's whole face warmed when he answered, really warmed, and he talked low and easy at the window, *he's great, Lib, you'd love him*, and at the end he said, "Love you, Lib," and it was warm and it was flat, both, like a hand on your shoulder through a winter coat.

He shrugged into his blazer. A square of folded paper slid out of the inside pocket and landed on the rug between them. Cal picked it up. MapQuest, the little logo at the top, turn-by-turn in a column: Route 10 south, then I-91 south, and at the bottom, Pleasant St, Northampton, MA. *Total Est. Time: 45 minutes.*

Teddy took it out of his hand a little fast and laughed a little early. "Sig Rho alumni dinner. It's in Northampton. Don't ask, it's a whole thing." He tucked it back in the blazer. "Dad's already on 91. Greenwich by midnight. He hates the traffic."
Cal didn't ask. When Patrick was eight he'd told three bigger kids on Gold Street that the lump under his jacket was a sweatshirt. It was a kitten. He'd used exactly that voice.

Henry took him the long way, down Elm Row, because he said it was instructive. The fraternity houses sat back on their lawns like old men on porches, and from an open third-floor window of a brick box with a beer garden out back, somebody had speakers turned to face the street.

body.text: Three guys in visors were on the porch roof with a funnel.

"Kappa Phi Tau," Henry said, without looking up. "1921. Disciplinary probation four times since 1988. I'd like to note that's a record." He walked faster than Cal expected, short quick steps, his notebook in his hand now instead of his pocket. "River Street was the ferry road until the bridge in 1851. That house was the ferryman's. A dentist owns it."
"How long have you been here?"

"Since I was six. Summers. My father's kept the grounds since 1976." Henry pushed his glasses up. "I know where most of the doors are. I've never walked anyone down here before. I've walked down here."

The street ended at the bluff, and at the end of the street was the Ferryhouse. Up close it was worse. Dark granite, no windows at all, not one, a cube somebody had dropped on the grass and walked away from. Over the door an Egyptian lintel, a winged disc going green. The door was iron, with an oar carved into it, blade up, and above that two words cut deep enough to hold shadow at dusk.
OBLIVIO FIDES.
"Club for dead people," Cal said.
"That was a joke. Mostly." Henry wiped his glasses on the hem of his shirt. "*Oblivio fides*. Forgetting is faith."
"That's a hell of a thing to carve over your front door."
"It's said that some of the seniors at the Corinthian tonight have keys to it." Henry tapped the notebook twice. "I can't source that. I'm telling you it's said."
"Which seniors?"
"That's what the door is for."

They walked past it to the edge of the bluff. Below, the Calder came out of the trees and went over the Ladder, an old mill dam the full width of the river with an iron fish ladder up one side like a fire escape for something that never learned to climb. The water went white over the lip and loud, then fell into the Connecticut and spread out wide and slow and copper. Down at the near bank was a pull-off for cars, and past it a path to the rocks, and across the path ran new chain-link, so new it held the last pink of the sky like tinfoil. On the fence, near the gate, was a small cluster of color. Red, a little white, something that caught light. Too far to make out.
Henry didn't look at it. He looked at the island.
It sat mid-river below the mouth of the Calder, long and dark with pines, and there were lights on in the trees. A lodge. A dock.
"What's that?"
"Gallows Island."
"Who'd they hang?"
"Nobody, officially. It might be a corruption of a Pocumtuck word, or it might not. The sources fight." He paused. "The island's private."
"Whose?"
"Theirs." Henry didn't turn his head toward the Ferryhouse. He didn't have to. Then he took his glasses off and cleaned them again, though they were clean.

"You looked at the river this morning," Henry said. "When I said it. Everyone else looked at the fridge." He put the glasses back on. "Josette Lavoie. Jo. She was twenty. She was studying nursing at Holyoke Community. The *Gazette* said she went swimming at the Ladder."
Cal looked down at the white water. Nobody would go in there. Nobody who'd ever been in water.
"You don't think so."
"I don't think things. I write them down." Henry's pen didn't move. "My father says the river keeps what it takes."
At the corner of River Street Henry said, quickly, as if he'd been holding it the whole way, "Thank you for coming."
"You didn't ask," Cal said. "You pointed."
"Yes," said Henry. "That's how I ask."

then.text: Cal took the stairs two at a time with the Race still on his resoled shoes, sixty years of spilled beer in the floorboards, and found Teddy at the mirror.

Teddy had changed his mind about the blazer twice more and then changed it back, and now he stood at the mirror, done.

body.text: He was ready, laughing at something nobody had said, and he pressed a card into Cal's hand. Heavy cream stock, the edges gilt, engraved so deep you could read it with your thumb: THE CORINTHIAN. FIRST LIGHT. *Mr. Theodore Vanderhoef IV.*
"Go be me," Teddy said. "I dare you. Just don't fuck anyone I'm related to."
"How would I know?"

"Assume everyone. Statistically you'll be right." He pulled the navy-and-white tie off over his head without loosening the knot and dropped the loop around Cal's neck. "The door reads ties." He left his collar open and spun his Saab keys once on a finger. "I'm off. Sig Rho, Dad's friends. If I'm not back by Christmas, tell my mother I died doing what I loved, which was nodding."

Third, for the record, you said there might be Kennedys. Did you meet any? You said there might be Kennedys. Also, have you seen the professors yet? Are any of them famous? Okay. That's four things. Bye.

Patrick hadn't said hi. Patrick didn't say hi on phones; he breathed at them. Siobhan had said it for him, the way she signed Ma's name to his permission slips. Cal had thirty-one minutes left on the card and did the math on them and put the phone in his blazer.
On the shelf over his desk the twins squinted at him from Castle Island, Siobhan holding her cone out like evidence, Patrick wearing most of his.
He turned off the lamp, then turned it back on, because Teddy would want a light when he came home, and went.

Fourteen Prospect Street was a Greek Revival temple somebody had talked into being a house: six white columns, a pediment like a raised eyebrow, a black door with no knob on the outside. Brick walls ran from both corners and hid a garden full of men laughing at a volume that assumed nobody would ever call the cops.

The door opened before he knocked. The member behind it was maybe twenty-one, pink from the heat, in a bottle-green blazer with brass buttons that caught the porch light like coins in a fountain. Past his shoulder, through the hall and out across a terrace, Cal counted the same green on thirty backs, same brass, a little gold column stitched over every heart. The guests wore navy. The members wore the club.
The kid took the engraved card and read it, then read Cal's face, then read the tie, and the tie was what did it. His eyes stayed on the stripe longest.
"Vanderhoef," he said, and stood aside. "Welcome home."

Inside smelled of lemon oil and cigars. Below the terrace the garden was laid out in boxwood, clipped knots and diamonds, with hurricane lanterns burning along every ledge of the wall. A jazz trio in white dinner jackets played for nobody in particular.
"*Vanderhoef!*"

It came across the terrace like a thrown drink, from a soft-faced senior in green holding court by the balustrade, a glass in each hand and his tie already a souvenir. "Archie Whitby," said the kid at the door, at Cal's shoulder. "President. He's been president since noon." Everyone near Archie laughed a half-second before he finished.

Cal heard the name. He even registered it as a nice old Dutch one, the kind that went on boathouses. A full second later he remembered it was his, and turned, and lifted his hand, and grinned like a man who'd waited all summer to be yelled at. Archie roared approval and went back to his court.

The second had already happened, though. Cal felt it on the back of his neck, the way you feel a hand near your wallet on a crowded Red Line car, and when he looked around, all he could see was green.

The members' bar was a mahogany counter in a paneled room off the terrace, under a hunting print of men in red coats killing something for sport. Nobody was tending it. Owen Tierney was, sort of. He'd come around behind it in the club's bottle-green blazer, a Student Assembly pin on the lapel, pouring for himself and whatever freshmen drifted close enough, humming under his breath.
Cal knew the tune before he knew he knew it. *The Parting Glass.* Three hours ago Owen had quoted a line of it to the whole chapel and gotten a laugh.

"Teddy," Owen said, and his face did the thing it had done from the pulpit: sandy-red hair, a field of freckles, a grin with the whole Kennedy family in it. The grin had a second layer, and the second layer said *I know exactly who you are, and I think it's great.* "What'll it be? And don't say a Cosmo, I'll have to report you to your father."
"Whatever you're having."

"Good man." Owen reached for the Jameson without looking, the way Patty reached for the Jameson at the Quiet Man, and poured two fingers and then a little more for luck. "You're a St. Brigid's kid. No, sorry." He laughed at himself. "You remind me of a kid I knew."
The floor went a degree off level.

St. Brigid's was his parish. He'd been baptized there and had served the seven o'clock Mass for two years in a cassock that stopped at his shins. For a second the whole Corinthian looked like a set somebody could strike in an afternoon.

Then he did the math the way you do when you want a particular answer. Every Irish kid in Boston with black hair and a fresh scar looked like a kid somebody knew. And Owen was lovely. That was the evidence. Owen was standing behind a rich men's bar in resoled Aldens, and Cal knew those soles, because he'd paid a cobbler on West Broadway for the same job twice.
"Common face," Cal said.

"Not that common." Owen slid the glass over. A white rope burn crossed his right palm, a stripe of slick new skin from the heel of his hand to the base of his fingers, healing but not healed. When he took his hand back he rubbed the stripe with his thumb, once, like it itched. His eyes went to Cal's eyebrow for half a second and then came back up, easy, warm, interested.
"Drink that slow. I'd stay and make sure, but I can't stay late. Early meeting." He raised his own glass an inch. "Assembly budget. The most thrilling document in New England."

then.text: "It's Cal," he said. "Reardon. Gold Street. You had the parish right. You just got the kid wrong."

Owen didn't blink. He looked, if anything, relieved, like a man who'd been holding a door and could finally let it go. "Cal Reardon, Gold Street." He said it back slowly, like tasting it, and a little Dorchester came up through the polish. "Listen to me, kid. Haverford Scholars find each other. Julian said there'd be a new one." He tapped the bar twice, a little benediction. "Your secret's safe. Be Teddy tonight. God knows Teddy could use the help."
"Never been to Boston," Cal said, in Teddy's voice, with Teddy's little laugh coming early. "Well. Once. She was a nice girl. I never called."

else.text: "Brigid's," Cal said, in the closest thing he had to Teddy's voice, which was mostly Teddy's laugh, coming early. "Is that a club? I think my mother's on the board."

then.text: Owen was delighted. He leaned on the bar to enjoy it. "And how's your father, Teddy?"
"Rich. Loud. Mostly in other rooms."
"Give him my best." Owen winked, slow, so Cal couldn't possibly miss it.
"What happened to your hand?"
Owen looked at his palm like it belonged to a guy he'd only just met. "Sailing," he said, and smiled. "I'm terrible."

body.text: Somebody in green clapped Owen on the shoulder and Owen leaned into it the way a politician leans into weather, delighted and damp, already laughing, already using the guy's name. Over his shoulder he said, "Music's upstairs. Money's on the terrace. Here's what I'd do," and then he was gone into the crowd without saying what he'd do.
Cal held the Jameson by the bowl of the glass and drank it slow.

body.text: The line for the second-floor bathroom ran halfway down the hall, and through the door came guitars, tinny and furious.

The bathroom was bigger than Cal's kitchen on Gold Street: black-and-white tile, a clawfoot tub full of ice and Heineken, a white Bose SoundDock on the toilet tank playing to the porcelain. At the sink a wiry kid with dark shaggy hair was doing business like a pharmacist. Narrow black jacket, buttoned, in the heat. Black nail polish chipped down to islands. His stock was laid out on a monogrammed hand towel, folded paper packets and a credit card, with the cash in the soap dish.
"Next," he said.
"Vanderhoef," said the member ahead of Cal, pointing back at him, a social courtesy.
The kid looked up. He took Cal in from the tie to the shoes and back up, slowly, the way you read a menu in a language you speak better than the waiter.
"Teddy Vanderhoef? I've met Teddy Vanderhoef. Southampton, two summers ago, a regatta that was really a hostage situation." He gave the name a little wave, like smoke. "He's taller and sadder."
Cal had his mouth open to sell it. The kid held up one painted finger.

"No. Don't. You'll ruin it." He was grinning now, wide, like a child at a magic show who has just seen exactly where the coin went. "I'm Rafe, and I will tell no one. Not out of loyalty, I've never had the stamina for loyalty. But nobody else in this building deserves it as much as I do."

His phone buzzed against the marble, a silver Razr doing a little dance. He looked at the screen and his face did something fast and private and then got very bright. He flipped it open and put it on speaker and held it up to the room.
"Mémère. You're on with the Corinthian Club bathroom, say hello."
An old woman's voice came out of the phone, low and amused and made of cigarettes. "*Raphaël.* Turn down that noise."
"The mayor just told the whole city to leave, Mémère. On television. I watched him."
"He said voluntary."
"Voluntary means *you*. Voluntarily. You, in the car, on I-10, eating a praline."

"I have been through Betsy, and I have been through Camille," said the phone, "and I will be through this one with a bottle of Sazerac and my rosary, and you will call me Monday and apologize." Then, in French, something that made Rafe close his eyes.

"She's hung up on me," he told the room, and everybody laughed, and he laughed loudest, a long looping laugh with a hiccup in the middle. He snapped the Razr shut. Cal watched his hand. It was shaking, a fine fast shiver, and Rafe looked at it like it was somebody else's and put it in his pocket.
Then he sold the sophomore a gram, counted the change out of the soap dish, and offered Cal the corner of a credit card with a little white hill on it.
"On the house. For your performance."
"Teddy's a lightweight," Cal said. "Two Smirnoff Ices and he cries about rowing."
Rafe considered this with real respect. "That's so specific I believe it." He tipped the card back over the towel. "Rain check, Theodore."
Cal went back out past the line with nothing in him but one slow Jameson and an old woman's voice saying *voluntary* like it was a dirty word.

The money stood at the bright end of the terrace in a loose horseshoe around Archie Whitby: Sig Rho legacies with lacrosse necks, two seniors in green arguing about a yacht like it was a horse, somebody's uncle. They opened the horseshoe for the tie and closed it behind him.

"Vanderhoef, old boy," Archie said, and handed him a fresh glass out of thin air. "Thank God. Tell them the one about your father and the Danforth boathouse. Nobody believes me. I tell it frightfully badly. I tell everything badly."
Cal had never heard of the Danforth boathouse. He knew Danforth was across the river and in New Hampshire, and that was all he knew.
"Which version?" he said. "The one he tells at Christmas, or the true one?"

The horseshoe tightened. He gave them 1978 and a full moon, Theodore Vanderhoef III and three Sig Rho brothers rowing a borrowed skiff upriver at two in the morning with a can of Hollis-green paint, in through the coxswain's window, out with every Danforth oar. "Here's the part he leaves out at Christmas," Cal said. "You can't swim with eight oars. So they stole the shell too. Four drunk guys rowing an eight. Forty minutes in circles. Danforth's crew came down to the dock and applauded."
"*No*," said a legacy.
"He sent them a thank-you note. On the firm's stationery. Danforth framed it. It's in their boathouse right now, if you know where to look."
"That's not how my father tells it," said a senior in green, frowning.
"Your father was in the boat," Cal said. "He's the one who kept going in circles."

The horseshoe came apart. Archie laughed hardest, a high delighted bray, and slapped the balustrade, and Cal could watch him filing it word for word for the next party, a story made up in forty seconds already on its way into the record. It was the best he'd felt all day, and it felt the way a stolen Slim Jim tastes: great, for about four seconds.

"That," Archie said, wiping his eyes, "goes in the book. Do you know about the lantern? Of course you don't, you're new. On the library mantel. Brass, ugly as sin. We light it once a year, tonight, First Light. The first Corinthian carried it out of the fire of 1832 with his eyebrows on fire, and he never let anyone forget it, and neither do we. Hence the party. We're commemorating a man who would not shut up."
Cal laughed in the right place and stopped listening, because a server had come through the horseshoe.

White shirt, black pants, a black apron with a name tape over the pocket: JO. She was carrying four champagne flutes in one hand, stems laced through her fingers, and she lifted two empties off the balustrade with the other without stopping. At the next table she stacked a busboy's plates for him before he'd figured out where to put them. When a member's elbow tipped a tray behind her she turned and caught the tray's edge with her hip, flat, without looking, and kept moving.
Cal knew that. He knew it the way you'd hear your own accent in a foreign airport. The rich kids who waited tables for a lark at the Cape did it like a game they could quit. She did it like rent.

She never came to the bright end. Every time she crossed the terrace she kept to the lanterns' blind side, her face turned toward the garden. Blonde, hair up. He tried twice to catch it and caught only the back of her neck.

Archie got up on a chair, which went about how you'd expect, and the trio stopped mid-bar. "Members. Guests. People who will be guests for the rest of their lives. Our toast is given by an honorary member who wrote speeches for a President, which is why he won't let me write mine. Professor Sloane."

The man who stepped up beside the chair didn't need it. He was forty or so, lean gone soft at the middle, in rumpled tweed nobody sane would wear in August, black hair silvering at the temples. An old steel watch sat loose on his wrist, the kind a man wears because somebody died. He held his glass in his left hand. The terrace quieted for him in a way it hadn't for Archie.

Servers came through with the toast trays. One stopped at Cal's elbow and he took a flute and looked her in the eye, the way he'd have looked at Bonnie or at Patty or at anybody holding a tray, because you did.
"Thanks, Jo," he said. He'd read the apron.
She froze. The tray stopped dead and the flutes on it shivered. Her face, for one second, went somewhere he couldn't follow, like he'd said something in a language only she spoke.

then.text: *Jo.* Three hours ago, the name had been on masking tape on a pickle jar by the Race's register. It caught in him and passed. It was a common name. It was a short one.
*Jo.* Henry's voice at the bluff, three hours back: *Josette Lavoie. Jo. She was twenty.* It caught in him and passed. It was a common name, and a short one.

It was the four-flute girl. Up close, in the lantern light she'd been dodging, she was the blonde from Bramwell's steps, the one with the steamer trunk and no parents and the eyebrow. He had the first word of it ready, *you're*, and didn't say it.

else.text: Up close, something about her was familiar, the line of her jaw or the angle she held her head. He couldn't place it, and he was good at placing faces.

body.text: Sloane raised his glass.
"The first lie Hollis will tell you," he said, "is that you belong here. The second is that you don't." He let the terrace wait. "Spend four years deciding which one to believe."

He drank, and they drank, and they cheered him the way people cheer when they aren't sure they've been complimented. His eyes passed over the crowd. They were pale gray-blue, the color of the river under haze, and they didn't seem to land anywhere long.

then.text: "*Vanderhoef!*" Archie, from the chair. "Tell the Professor the boathouse one!"

else.text: "*Vanderhoef!*" Archie, from the chair, for no reason at all. "Greenwich! Come meet the Professor!"

body.text: The full second again. Cal heard it, and then remembered it was his, and then turned. The server was looking right at him while he did it. She saw the whole second go by. Then she turned with her tray and was gone into the house, and the place where she'd been standing was just terrace.
The crowd shifted and dropped Cal at the members' bar, at Sloane's elbow, the two of them facing the same row of bottles. Sloane didn't look at him.
"Vanderhoef," he said. "You don't sound like Greenwich."

then.text: "Boarding school," Cal said, easy. "It kills the accent. My mother still cries about it. She says I sound like a scholarship boy." He gave it Teddy's laugh, early.
"Her hip's titanium, so the crying's mostly structural."

then.text: Cal touched the eyebrow without noticing, and Sloane's eyes followed the hand.

Sloane's mouth went crooked on one side. "Then you're better at this than your father." He lifted his glass an inch. "I wrote speeches for a President for four years, Mr. Vanderhoef. The best liars all have one thing in common. They enjoy it a little less than you do." He let that sit one beat too long, as if he'd heard himself.
He didn't know why he did it. The toast, maybe. "I'm Cal Reardon," he said. "South Boston. The tie's on loan."

Sloane didn't answer. The trio started again behind them. He set his glass down on the mahogany and turned it a quarter turn by the stem with his left hand, and the pause went on long enough that Cal started composing an exit.
"I knew a Reardon once," Sloane said. "Long time ago." Then he picked the glass back up. "Nobody here is supposed to be here, Mr. Reardon. Enjoy it."
"I'm not lying," Cal said. "I'm workshopping."
Sloane laughed, a real one, surprised out of him. "Then take my seminar. HUM 117. The Uses of Lying. Wednesdays, two o'clock. Bring that."

body.text: He looked at Cal then, finally, straight on, and held it a moment longer than a stranger would, the way you'd look twice at a word you'd spelled right and suddenly weren't sure of. Then three men in green came at him with their hands out, *Nate*, *Professor*, *you have to settle something*, and the members closed around him and he was gone.

The Corinthian's kitchen had been built in 1832 for a staff of nine, and tonight it was running on fourteen, plus a radio gaffer-taped over the Hobart that pulled in one station out of Springfield, and the station had decided it was Mariah's world and the rest of them were just sweating in it. The alley door was propped with a milk crate, and the night coming through it was hotter than the room.

Here she was Dee. Pioneer Valley Catering had hired Dee on Thursday without asking for much beyond black pants and a pulse, because they were short since the Lavoie girl, and the woman with the clipboard had said it the way you'd say the ice machine was down.

At six, behind the van, Captain Bev Szalinski, fifty-some, with a laugh like gravel going down a chute, had dug a spare apron out of a bin and tossed it to her. Black bib, PVC stitched over the heart, and under that a strip of label tape with two white letters punched into it. JO.
Del had looked at it exactly as long as it took to tie the strings. Then she had decided not to think about it, which was a thing she did well.

Four minutes into the crab cakes she was the best server in the building, and the only person who knew it was Del, which was the point. A good server was a temperature, not a person. She took the swinging door on the out side, always the out side, tray high. She carried four flutes by the stems in one hand like a bouquet she didn't want. On the terrace she worked the dark end, and faces under the hurricane lanterns looked at the tray and never at the girl. She had built the whole night on that.
At the dish pit Marco was scraping plates and talking low. "She worked the island thing for us. That Saturday. Bev put her on it."
"And now they're saying she went swimming at the Ladder." Tina had a bus tub on her hip and her jaw out. "Jo couldn't swim for shit. She'd never."
"She was seeing somebody up here."
Tina turned toward the clipboard. "Bev, they didn't even send flowers."
Bev didn't look up. "Lower your voices."
Tina's eyes snagged on the tape on Del's chest and slid off it, fast, like a hand off a pan.
Del topped off six flutes and thought about nothing, beautifully. Mariah wanted to know when the man was coming back. Get in line, lady.

The swinging door went out on Marco's shoulder, and on the backswing she could see across the hall into the library. A tall young man, dark blond, stood alone at the window with a club soda, his left hand wrapped in a white bandage, looking at the river as if it owed him something.
She knew the face. She knew the name that went with it.
Her hands went still on the tray. The flutes didn't even ring.

choices.label: Ask whose apron this was.
Head down. Be the best one here.
Lift the guest list off Bev's clipboard.
Take the library tray. Walk right past him.

body.text: She asked the way you'd ask about the weather, plucking at the bib with two fingers on her way past the pass. "Whose was this, anyway? It's got a name on it."
"That's—" Tina said.
"Van spare," said Bev, still not looking up. "Terrace, Dee."

So Del did the terrace. She did it twice. When she came back the second time Tina was in the walk-in, hauling a case of the members' Veuve off the bottom rack, and Del slipped in behind her to help, and the door sighed shut on the two of them and the cold.

Tina talked fast and low, like the shelves might be listening. "She took pictures of everything. One of those cardboard cameras from the drugstore. The food, us, the members. The Hollis kids thought it was cute." She got her end of the case up. "And she was seeing a Hollis boy. She wouldn't say who. Said it like she'd won something."
Their breath smoked. Tina looked at the tape again and this time didn't look away.

Upstairs, in a canvas tote at the back of a linen closet, there was a secondhand Polaroid that Del used to photograph everything that wasn't her. She thought about that, and about the tape, and understood that she might be wearing a dead girl's name.
She didn't take it off. Nobody remembers an apron. Everybody remembers the girl who took hers off halfway through a party.
Bev leaned into the walk-in. "Sloane's toast. Terrace. Go."
Del lifted the toast tray, and the cold came out with her.
She put her head down and was magnificent, and nobody saw it, which was how you knew.

She cleared a table of six without a clink. She caught a fork going off a plate with the side of her wrist and had it in her apron pocket before the man who'd dropped it noticed it was gone. When a sophomore in seersucker backed into her, she turned with him like a dance partner and the tray never tipped. She refilled water before anyone thought the word *water*. Tina stopped watching her and started copying her, and Marco said "Jesus, Dee" in a tone that was almost hurt. Twice she crossed the hall and twice did not look through the library door, which took more than the trays.
At ten past ten Bev was in the alley doorway lighting a Marlboro Light off the last of the old one, blowing the smoke out into the dark like a courtesy to the building.
"Where'd PVC find you?"
"Thursday."
Bev laughed, the gravel going down. "You've done this before."
"Never," Del said, and gave her the smile that went with it. Her thumb went to her left wrist for something to turn and found bare skin.

"Kid, you hold four flutes like my mother. Forty years of weddings and she never spilled on a bride." Bev pulled the clipboard off the crate, wrote something next to DEE, and underlined it twice. Del didn't like that at all.
"Sloane's toast. Terrace. Go."

Del lifted the toast tray. Through the terrace doors, at the bright end where she never went, a dark-haired boy in a striped tie stood with his blazer sleeves an inch short, laughing at something, holding his glass by the bowl.
Somebody's tie, she thought. Not his.

The clipboard lay on the steel counter by the warming cabinet while Bev was in the walk-in yelling about lemons. Three sheets, typed, stapled at the corner, FIRST LIGHT — MEMBERS AND GUESTS in small capitals at the top. Nobody was looking at the counter. Nobody ever looked at the counter.

Del set her empty tray down on it, picked her empty tray back up, and the pages came with it, flat against the underside under her spread fingers. She went out the back way, up the service stairs two at a time in her flat black shoes, and down the second-floor hall to the linen closet.

Inside it smelled like starch and cedar. Behind the stacked tablecloths, where she had left it at six, was the canvas tote, and in the tote, folded in tissue, the green silk. She pulled the string on the bulb and gave herself ten seconds.
Ashford, G.
Tierney, O.
Sloane, N. (Hon.)
Whitby, A.
Vanderhoef, T. IV (legacy)

There were sixty names. Only one of them was a freshman, and he had a little word in brackets after him that meant every old man downstairs had known his father since prep school. She ran her eye back up to the top of the first page, to the first name, and held it there a second longer than she'd meant to.
Then the bulb went off, the pages went into the tote beside the dress waiting in tissue, and Dee went back down the stairs.
Bev was patting the counter where the clipboard should have been, frowning at it like it had moved on purpose. "Sloane's toast. Terrace. Go."
Del lifted the toast tray.
"Library wants a club soda," Bev said, "with lime, no ice, he was very particular about the no ice," and Tina reached for it, and Del got there first.
She went across the hall at a server's pace, the glass on a little silver tray, the cocktail napkin squared. Never hurry into a room. Hurrying says you're afraid of it.

The library was leather and old smoke and men in oil paint who had never carried anything heavier than a grudge. A brass lantern sat on the mantel, polished by somebody paid by the hour, the only object in the room that looked like it had been somewhere. Past the window the river was black.
She came up on his right, the unbandaged side. She set the glass on the sill by his good hand, close enough to smell the lime.
"Thank you," he said, to the window.
He never turned his head. She was a hand and a small cold weight arriving where he wanted it.

Relief came up through her like the first breath after a dive, and the insult came up right behind it, in the same breath, so close she couldn't have pulled them apart with tweezers. Nobody here looked at the staff. She'd bet her whole night on it. It was still a hell of a thing to win.
On her way out she looked at the lantern once, the way you look at a door you might need later.
Back in the kitchen, Bev was already holding out the toast tray. "Sloane's toast. Terrace. Go."
Del lifted it. Her hands were perfectly steady, which she resented.

She had been ready for the photograph in its Ziploc. She had been ready, more or less, for the candles in jelly jars, the Red Sox cap gone pale at the brim, the plastic roses that would never die because they'd never lived, the rosary looped on the chain-link like something hung out to dry. She read the oar blade twice and filed it.

then.text: *A Hollis boy, she wouldn't say who.* Del looked along the fence for a cardboard camera. There wasn't one.
A G. A tall man with a bandaged hand and a club soda, who had never turned his head.
A G. at the bottom of an apology. A G. at the top of a typed list, folded in her tote. She filed that, too, and didn't like where she put it.

It was pinned through the fence at about the height of a girl's heart: PVC CATERING, and under it a strip of label tape in the same punched white capitals she'd worn on her chest since six o'clock. JO.

She didn't let it finish.
Cal stood beside her with candlelight on his ridiculous borrowed tie, the boy who had looked her in the eye on the terrace and said *Thanks, Jo* like it was only manners.

body.text: At ten past five Sutter 304 had been the blue of skim milk, and Cal had been asleep with one arm thrown over his face like a man ducking a photographer. So she'd been one. She clicked on the desk lamp, took a single picture, waited for it to come up out of the gray, and wrote on the back with his pen. She took the stack of laundry quarters he'd built by the lamp, and his gray hoodie off the chair, and the watch from where it lay face down on his desk. Then she stood in the doorway with her shoes in her hand.
She didn't wake him. Nobody needed to see her face in daylight yet.

Now she stood barefoot on the depot's tile with the green silk under a Southie boy's sweatshirt and her heels hooked on two fingers. The ticket window had its shutter down. A man in a Peter Pan polo was mopping the far end in slow figure eights, and the place smelled of Pine-Sol and diesel.

Over the ticket counter a TV was on CNN with the sound almost off. The banner said the storm had been upgraded overnight. The cone lay across the bottom of the map, white and widening, its mouth open over the Gulf.

She'd meant to walk past it. She stood under it instead, sleeves pulled down over her hands, while the satellite loop turned the same pinwheel again and again. All day yesterday it had been somebody else's. She knew that shoreline the way you know the ceiling over your own bed.

then.text: For no reason she would have admitted to, she thought of two kids in a photograph on a dorm-room wall.

body.text: Three pay phones by the restrooms, one with no receiver, just a steel cord. She took the middle one.

She fed in Cal's quarters, his laundry going down the slot. Her finger found the buttons without her. One. Two. Two. Eight. The rest she didn't need to look at. A recorded woman asked for two dollars and forty cents, and Del fed her quarter after quarter until the slot stopped complaining, and then it rang. Four times. Five.
A boy, thick with sleep, his voice lower than the last time she'd heard it.
She did not let herself think his name.
