body.text: When it came out, it didn't come out in the voice she had built. It came out low and slow and wide open, the vowels taking their time, a voice nobody in Calder Falls had ever heard.
"It's me."
Breathing on the line. A bedspring.
"Listen to me. Y'all need to go north. Today. Now. Don't wait on it." She pressed her forehead to the cool steel of the phone box. "Tell her I said. Tell her I'll send money."
"Where are you?"
She looked at the man with the mop, at the green silk under a borrowed sweatshirt, at the morning coming up gray and already warm through the glass.
"Someplace cold," she said, and hung up before the recorded woman could ask her for anything else.
Then she turned the watch on her wrist, once, all the way around, and went out into the street with her shoes in her hand.
She opened her mouth and nothing in it was the right voice.
"'Lo?" the boy said again. A pause, a rustle of sheets. "Hello?"
She stood there and breathed. Over the counter the satellite loop came around again, the same white pinwheel, patient as a drain.
On the other end it went quiet, the kind of quiet a person makes when they're holding the phone away from their ear to look at it. Then he came back, closer, softer.
"Is that you?"
She put the receiver back in its cradle the way you set down a pan you didn't know was hot, fast and careful at once, as if it might still bite.
The promise of money stayed in her mouth. She kept it there. It tasted like the quarters.
The man with the mop had stopped to look at the TV too. Neither of them said anything. Del turned the watch on her wrist, once, all the way around, and walked out into the gray.

then.text: The man who caught him at the foot of the main stairs had the canned ham face Teddy had promised him, down to the belt with the little green whales.

else.text: The man who caught him at the foot of the main stairs had a face like a boiled ham and a belt with little green whales on it.

body.text: "Teddy *Vanderhoef*. Kip Lyman. I roomed with your father freshman year, God help me." He didn't let go of the hand. "Last time I saw you, you bit my wife. You were four. How's your mother's hip?"

then.text: "Titanium and furious," Cal said.

Kip threw his head back. "That's *Bunny*. God, that's Bunny to the life." He wanted more, and Cal had it all in his pocket like rolled quarters: Commodore, eleven, never once wrong about a person; Round Hill; the city, meaning New York, meaning always. Every right answer put him deeper into a story Kip would be telling by lunch tomorrow.

else.text: "Better," Cal said. "She's got a cane. A really nice cane. She hates it."
Kip squinted. Not suspicion, not yet: a man checking his coat-check ticket against the coat. "Bunny with a cane. I'd pay money."
"It's got a duck on the handle," Cal said, and wanted to die.

body.text: "Let's ring your father!"

The Razr was out before Cal could invent a reason not to. Kip held it at arm's length, squinting down his own arm, and somewhere in Greenwich a phone rang four times. Kip's face fell and lit right back up, because voicemail was an audience too.
"Theo! Kip. I'm with your boy at First Light, he's got your chin, God help him. Call me. We'll do Round Hill." He snapped it shut. "He'll love that."

While Kip waved somebody over to admire the chin, Cal said, "Gents'," took the stairs two at a time, and on the second-floor landing went through a green baize door marked PRIVATE like a man who'd been told to.

Behind it the Corinthian stopped pretending: bare bulbs, linoleum, a dumbwaiter, starch. A closet door swung open and a girl came out backward with a beaded evening bag in her teeth, reaching behind herself for a zipper.

Green silk. That was all he'd have been able to say about it later, under oath. Pearls. A gold watch with a square face, loose on a thin wrist. Hair down, the sun still in it. A canvas tote on one shoulder that didn't go with any of it.
She turned around and saw him.
*Oh*, he thought, and watched her think it too.
She took the bag out of her mouth. "Zip me or leave."

She gave him her back. He drew the zip up slowly from the small of her back, over the knobs of her spine, and she lifted her hair off her neck to let him finish. Under the perfume she smelled like the kitchen. His knuckles touched skin once. Neither of them mentioned it.
"Jo," he said, to the back of her neck. "Four flutes, no spills."
"And you're Teddy Vanderhoef."
"How'd you know I'm not?"
She stepped back and counted him off on her fingers, which was his move, and he resented it immediately.

"You thanked the help. Nobody here thanks the help. You hold your glass by the bowl, like it's a beer that got promoted. That's a very good tie on a boy whose shoes were resoled in somebody's basement." The fourth finger. "And you answer to Teddy like it's a dog you're walking."

then.text: A thumb. "And Teddy Vanderhoef is on the list as a legacy, which means half the old men here have met him, and one of them is going to ask about his mother's hip."
*One already had*, Cal thought.

choices.label: Read her back, tell for tell.
Laugh. Give her the win.
Deny everything. Badly.

then.text: "The apron," Cal said. "It's in that bag. Black, with a name on the tape, and the name's not yours, because when I said it you froze like I'd read you your rights." He held up two fingers to her four. "You came out of a closet in a dress that costs more than my mother's car. And nobody who belongs here knows where the linen closet is."
Her face opened up like he'd tipped her forty percent.
"Oh," she said. "You're *that* one."
He laughed, his own laugh, from the stomach, the one that got him thrown out of CCD in sixth grade. "Okay. Okay. I'm a disgrace to Greenwich. Do the part about the shoes again. I'd pay."
She'd had her weight on her front foot for a fight. The laugh took the floor out from under her, and for a second she didn't know what to do with her hands.
"Here," she said finally, like she was giving him change. "One for free. You laugh half a second before they finish the joke, like you're cueing an audience. Real people wait. Let it come late."
Cal had picked that laugh up from Teddy, around the second hour of the Range Rover. He decided not to say where.
"I'm Teddy Vanderhoef," Cal said. "Of Greenwich. Connecticut."
"Nobody from Greenwich says Connecticut."
"I'm very thorough."
"And your vowels have a subway in them. Round them off. Lock your jaw. Talk like you've never once paid for parking."
So he did Greenwich again, worse, on purpose, jaw wired shut, every vowel off to a regatta. She laughed out loud and caught it with the back of her hand, furious at herself.

body.text: Feet on the back stairs, heavy, fast. "*Dee?*"
A woman in a catering polo came up with a cigarette behind her ear and a smoker's laugh already loading. Her eyes went over the girl in green the way you look past a lamp, and stopped on the tie.
"Sorry, hon. You seen a blonde server? Hair up, walks like she's late?"
"Can't say I have," Cal said, in his best Teddy. "Would you be a sweetheart? My father's coat is in the car. Black Range Rover, on Prospect. He gets a chill."
It was eighty-six degrees. "Sure, hon," she said, and went back down. He had just done to her what Theodore Vanderhoef III had done to him at the curb, and it had worked, and he didn't like how well.
The baize door banged. "*Vanderhoef!* Greenwich! Kip says you're the image of—"
A hand hooked through Cal's elbow.
"Teddy, *darling*," said the girl in green, in a voice that had summered somewhere with a lighthouse, "you promised you'd introduce me to your mother."
"Is Bunny *here*?" said Archie, to nobody, because she was already walking Cal away through a pantry full of silver and down the back stairs, past the roar of the kitchen, and down again.
The cold hit them on the last step like a hand on the chest. Stone, racks to the ceiling with the dust left on the bottles on purpose, one bulb on a cord.

She leaned against a rack and laughed with her whole body, and so did he, and every time one of them nearly stopped the other said *Bunny* or *coat*. She smacked his chest, hard, and he caught the wrist. He didn't let go. She didn't ask him to.
"You almost got me killed up there," she said.
"*I* almost got *you*—"
"You told Bev to go find a coat. In August."
"You told Archie Whitby my mother's in the building."
"Goddamn it," Del said, wiping her eyes with the heel of her hand, "I haven't laughed like that since—" She didn't finish it, and he didn't ask.
The bulb made one shadow of them on the floor. Her eyes were a light brown, almost gold, and they went to his mouth and came back up, deliberately, so he'd know.
"Here's how this goes," she said. "I never saw you. You never saw me."
"Swear."
"On what?"
She put one finger flat against the knot of Teddy's tie. "On whatever you've got."

choices.label: Swear on your mother.
Swear on Siobhan and Patrick.
choices.echo: You gave a stranger two names.

choices.label: Swear on nothing.

then.text: "I swear on my mother." It sat there too plain, so he added, "Which in my house is binding arbitration."

She studied him the way you'd hold a bill up to the light. Patty was behind a bar ninety miles east, two shifts past tired, and he meant it so plainly it embarrassed him. Whatever she saw, she nodded at it.
"I swear on Siobhan and Patrick."
It came out before he could check it. He never said their names out loud to anyone who didn't already know them.
"Who are Siobhan and Patrick?"
"People I don't swear on lightly."
She looked at him for a long moment. Then she let it go, and he watched her put it somewhere and close the drawer.
"I swear on nothing."
"That's not how it works."
"I don't swear on things I love," he said. "It's bad luck. Ask any priest in Boston."
She looked annoyed, and then she looked like she liked him for it a good deal more than she wanted to.

body.text: "Fine. Rule two," she said. "Whoever gets caught first owes the other one true thing."
She ran her hand along the racks without reading a label, like someone who'd read the cellar book, and drew out a bottle. Cal read it for her. KRUG. 1985.
"'85 was a good year," she said.
"Cal," he said. "Reardon." It seemed only fair.
"Reardon. Of course it is. Del."
"Del what?"
"Ashcombe."
He saw the page in the Matriculation Book, *Delphine E. Ashcombe*, three lines above his own name. It had sounded like a boat. "You signed the book at four."
The smallest pause. "Everybody signs the book."
"So why the apron?"
"Honestly?" She turned the gold watch once around her wrist. "I was bored."
He believed the name. He didn't believe the reason. Nobody got that good at a tray out of boredom.
"I know you from somewhere."
A wiry kid sat on the cellar stairs with the members' Lagavulin in his lap like a cat, black nail polish chipped to islands. He had obviously been there for the whole Krug.
He was looking at Del.
"Rehab?" said Del.
The kid put a hand over his heart. "Oh, I *like* you."

then.text: He swung to Cal, taking in the jacket, the tie. "Rafe. And you're Teddy Vanderhoef? I've met Teddy Vanderhoef. He's taller and sadder." His Razr buzzed on the step, *Mémère*, and his face did something fast and private, and he silenced it. "My grandmother," he said brightly. "She's being brave at a hurricane."

else.text: "Theodore," Rafe said to Cal, warmly, like they were old friends, which by Corinthian standards they were. "You found a friend."

body.text: He tucked the Lagavulin inside his jacket and stood. "I want you both to know I'm keeping this. Whatever this is. Somewhere cool and dark, like the wine." He went up two at a time, humming.

They came up into the heat like divers surfacing, the Krug cold against his ribs under the blazer. The terrace had gotten louder and looser. Somebody's tie was on the jazz bassist. At the far balustrade Sloane stood with Archie, nodding, not listening.
Del took Cal's arm as if she'd been doing it for years. In the dress, nobody looked twice at her.
A flash went off somewhere among the lanterns, white and sudden.
She turned her face from it like it had slapped her. Fast, and complete, chin to shoulder. Then she was back, smiling, as if she'd only been checking on the moon.
He didn't ask. She saw him not ask.
"All right, Teddy," she said, low, against his ear. "Prove you're good at this."

choices.label: Dare her to dance with Archie.
Dare her to kiss you. Right here.
Dare her over the garden wall. In that dress.

then.text: "Dance with Archie. Let him lead. It'll be the worst night of his life."
"Oh, that's cruel." She was already going.
She cut Archie out of his court with two fingers on his lapel and walked him backward onto the flagstones, and inside thirty seconds she owned him.
"Whose cousin's friend are you?" Archie asked, dazzled, trying to lead.
"Archie's."
"*I'm* Archie."
"I know, darling. That's how close we are."
Archie laughed so hard he stepped on her, and Cal watched her steer the president of the Corinthian around his own terrace like a shopping cart with a bad wheel.
"Kiss me. Right here. Let them wonder whose cousin I am."

She looked around at the people who ran Hollis, the green blazers and the old men, the trio back around to *Night and Day*. Then she put her hand flat on his chest over the Krug and kissed him in the middle of the terrace.

She did it like she was winning. Her mouth was cool from the cellar. Somewhere in the second chorus she stopped winning, and he felt her stop, felt her fingers close on his shirt, and it went somewhere neither of them had dared the other to. A member whistled through his teeth. She pulled back one inch and didn't open her eyes right away.
"Well," she said. "That's done, then."
It wasn't, and they both heard it.
"Over the garden wall," he said. "In that dress. I'll hold your shoes and be very supportive."
She looked at the garden wall, eight feet of old brick with lanterns along the top, and then at him, like a woman pricing a car.
"Later," she said. "I don't do dares on credit."
"That's not a no."
"It's not anything yet." She smiled. She was holding it, and she wanted him to watch her hold it.

body.text: "My turn." She leaned into his ear again. "Steal me something of theirs."

then.text: "The lantern," he said. "Library mantel. Brass, ugly as sin. Archie says a man carried it out of a fire in 1832 and never shut up about it."

else.text: "There's a lantern on the library mantel," she said. "Brass, older than God. They look at it like it's going to forgive them."

body.text: They went in through the hall. Owen Tierney was coming down the main stairs, flushed from the heat and the handshaking.

"Be good, Teddy," he said, passing, and pointed two fingers at Cal like a blessing. "Or be good at it." He gave Del a polite, pleasant nod, the nod for a nice girl he'd never met, and went out the front door into the dark.

Leather, dark wood, old men in oil paint who looked like they'd just been told the price of something and approved. On the mantel a brass lantern, squat and dented, its chimney smoked brown, a flame burning low inside. Beyond the tall window the river was black.
Someone was already in it.

He stood alone at the window with a club soda: tall, dark-blond, green-eyed, a jaw off a recruiting poster, his left hand bandaged to the wrist. The only sober person Cal had seen since nine. He turned and looked at Del a second too long.
"I'm sorry," he said. "Have we met?"
"Everyone says that," Del said, lightly. "Honestly, I think it's the cheekbones. You're Ashford, aren't you? Archie said there'd be a tall one with a boat."

then.text: Her hand tightened on Cal's arm, once, hard enough that he felt each finger. Her face didn't change at all.

else.text: Del's grip on his arm went light and exact, the way a hand goes when it has decided to be a glove. She didn't look at the window again.

body.text: The man looked at her a moment longer and then let it go, politely, the way you'd let go of a word on the tip of your tongue. He turned to Cal.
"You're not Teddy Vanderhoef."
Cal felt the Krug against his ribs and every lie he'd told since nine stacked up behind his teeth.

"I taught Teddy to sail when he was nine," the man said. "I was twelve and insufferable." He didn't sound angry. He sounded tired in a way that had nothing to do with the hour. "It's all right. I won't—it's all right. Take the bottle. Go out through the garden. The wall's lower by the fig tree."
He turned back to the river and drank his club soda and was done with them.
They were at the door when he spoke again, still facing the glass.
"Stay away from the river tonight."
The lantern burned on the mantel between them and the door, small and smug.

choices.label: Lift the lantern off the mantel.
Leave it. You've stolen enough tonight.

body.text: Boxwood clipped into knots and diamonds, hurricane lanterns guttering along the paths, the terrace falling away behind them. Down Elm Row a frat house had its windows open and its speakers up past reason.

then.text: He'd blown it out and stuck it under his blazer opposite the Krug. The brass was still warm. It knocked his hip every step and made him walk like a man with a bad one, and Del had to stop twice to laugh into her hand.

body.text: The fig leaned on the back wall, and the man had been right: the brick there was lower. Del handed Cal her bag, her tote, her shoes, like a woman checking her coat. She hitched the green silk to her thighs and went up the fig and onto the wall barefoot without once looking for a handhold, quick and quiet, like someone who'd needed to get over things, a long time ago, before anyone was watching. She didn't make a show of it. That was what he noticed.

then.text: On top she crouched, and he stood on the root of the fig with his arms full of her things, and she took his face in both hands and paid the dare. She kissed him from above, slow, the party at her back and the town in front of her.
"There," she said against his mouth. "Paid in full."

body.text: He threw her the shoes and the bags, then himself. They came down hard into the alley, onto gravel and somebody's recycling, and lay there in the dark laughing until it hurt, while the song went on without them.

Del sat up first, with a fig leaf in her hair and the Krug in her lap like a baby she'd rescued from a fire. Down the alley, past the last streetlight, under the song, there was another sound, low and steady, that didn't stop between verses.
"He said stay away from the river," she said.
"He did."
She found her shoes in the dark and stood up, holding them by the straps. "So which way is it?"

Main Street was on the way to the river, and empty, and still hot, the sidewalk giving the day back up through Cal's soles. They got as far as the diner before Del smelled fries and the river lost. The storefronts were dark except the Hollis Bookstore, where a light was on in the vestibule over a hand-lettered sign, 24-HOUR PHOTO KIOSK — MOVE-IN WEEKEND, and nobody inside. Del walked barefoot with her heels hooked on two fingers, and the green silk went black and green again under the streetlights.

The Calder Falls Diner stayed open till two on move-in weekend and said so in the window like a hostage note: OPEN LATE FOR HOLLIS FAMILIES. Red vinyl, a pie case, an SNL rerun with the sound off. The waitress was about his mother's age, with a pen stuck through her ponytail and LORRAINE on her blouse. She looked at the dress for a long, flat second. Then at the tie. Then at the shape under his blazer.
"Prom?"
"Wedding," Del said.
"Whose?"
"Undecided."
Lorraine brought two coffee mugs nobody had ordered and a brown paper bag, and set the bag on the seat beside Cal. "Whatever that is goes in there, and I didn't see it."
The Krug went in the bag. Under the table Cal eased the cork out with his thumbs, a pop no louder than a knuckle, and it went in the mugs.

then.text: The lantern stayed under his blazer, warm against his hip. Lorraine didn't have a bag that size.

body.text: Del ate fries like she'd come off a double. "I missed supper," she said, with her mouth full, reaching for the ketchup.
"Supper."
"Is there a problem?"
"My grandmother said supper. She also said 'the wireless' and thought Ted Williams was a saint."
"Ted Williams *was* a saint."
"Ted Williams is in a freezer in Arizona."
"So he's a saint who planned ahead."

When Lorraine came back the table was already cleared: fry basket nested in the pie plate, forks laid across, the stack slid to the corner where a waitress's hand would land. Lorraine looked at it, and then at Del, longer than she had at the dress. "Thanks, hon."
Then Del came up out of the tote with a secondhand Polaroid the size of a lunchbox, masking tape on the strap. "Don't move."
"I'm not..."
The flash went off. The camera ground out the print and she laid it face up between them, and they watched him come up out of the gray.

body.caption: Teddy Vanderhoef, allegedly.
body.text: Cal in the booth, Teddy's tie loosened, the Krug in a paper bag, the diner's neon behind him.
She uncapped a pen with her teeth and wrote along the white border.
"Now you." He reached for the camera.
It was back in the tote before his hand got there. "I don't photograph well."
"Have you seen you?"
"Often," Del said. "That's how I know."

The check came face down, seven dollars in pencil. Cal bent for the money in his sock, and when he came up there was a ten under the sugar jar and Del was looking out the window like it had arrived on its own.
"That's ten."
"Is it."
"On seven."
"Lorraine has a pen through her hair at midnight, Reardon. Lorraine can have three dollars."

She'd said the number out loud. Nobody with a watch like that said the number out loud. He'd watched rich people tip his mother his whole life, like it was a tax, and the ones who left three on seven had carried a tray. He put it with the supper and the stacked plates, three things with nowhere to go yet.
"Thanks, Lorraine," he said on the way out, and Del looked at him the way she had over the toast tray, and then she didn't.

A lopsided half-moon had come up over the New Hampshire hills, low and orange in the haze and bigger than it had any business being. River Street ran out of houses and turned into bluff, and at the end of it the Ferryhouse sat on the grass like something set down and forgotten, a black cube darker than the dark behind it.
"What's that?" Del said.
"A tomb."
"For who?"
"For whoever they want."

then.text: "There's words over the door. *Oblivio fides.*"
"Forgetting is faith," Del said, before he could.
He looked at her.
"Grandmother," she said. "She thought Latin was good for the posture."

else.text: "A kid with a notebook told me it's a club for dead people."
"Members only, I hope."

body.text: The dam road went down off the bluff in loose gravel between walls of sumac, and the Ladder came up to meet them, a hush and then a roar. Past it the Connecticut lay wide and silver, and mid-river sat the island, black with pines, one light in the trees.
Del turned and walked backward ahead of him, shoes swinging. "Bet I can beat you to the island."

then.text: "That's Gallows Island."
"Charming."

body.text: She was already reaching behind her for the zipper he'd done up at twenty to eleven. Then the road ended at new chain-link, bright as tinfoil under the moon, and a sign wired to it at eye level: NO SWIMMING — DANGER — CALDER FALLS POLICE.
Her hand came back down.

The gate was chained. The shrine started beside it and ran down the fence a few yards, the way those things did at home, where somebody taped a Mass card to a lamppost on Broadway and in a week the lamppost was wearing a whole life.

Somebody had lit the candles tonight. They stood in jelly jars along the gravel, most still going, low and gold in the glass. A graduation photo in a Ziploc, zip-tied to the chain-link and fogged on the inside. A Red Sox cap gone pink at the brim. Plastic roses wired through the diamonds. A rosary looped over a post. A name tag pinned through the fence. A card in a sandwich bag: *we love you Jo-Jo — HCC Nursing*.

And propped against the fence where the candles lit it best, the blade of a crew oar, sawn off at the neck, Hollis green. Somebody had lettered it in white house paint, carefully, and not carefully enough to stop the paint from running.
*J. — I'm sorry. — G.*
The girl in the photo had dark hair and freckles and a gap in her front teeth, and she was laughing at whoever held the camera with her whole face.

then.text: Cal knew the face. He'd seen it six hours ago over a cash register on Canal Street, next to a pickle jar that said FOR JO.
*Josette Lavoie,* Henry said in his head, in that voice like a card catalog. *Jo. She was twenty.*

body.text: "Kid on my floor told me. Wire glasses, notebook, looks like a tiny accountant who found God." He didn't smile. "He said they fenced the dam two weeks ago. A girl drowned."
Thirty yards off, the water went over the Ladder and kept saying the one thing it said.
He'd expected Del to come back with something quick. She didn't. She'd gone very still, and she was looking at the name tag.

then.text: "I wore her name tonight."
She said it plainly, the way you'd tell somebody the time. No *darling* on it.
Cal looked at the tag. PVC CATERING, and under it two white letters on black tape. He saw the terrace, the toast tray, his own mouth. "I called you by it."
"I know."
"I said thanks."
"I know that, too," Del said. "You were the only one who did."

else.text: She didn't say anything.

Cal looked at the tag, and then at her, and saw the apron on the terrace: the same white capitals, the same two letters. She knew exactly what she'd worn. He could watch her knowing it. Neither of them said it, and the not saying took up all the room along the fence.

body.text: They'd been drunk. The river had taken most of that and left them standing closer than strangers stand, the candle heat on his shins and her bare shoulder an inch from his sleeve.

then.text: He never knew which of them moved. She had her back to the chain-link a few yards down from the candles and his tie in her fist, Teddy's tie, and she kissed him like she was arguing with someone who wasn't there. The fence gave under her and rang softly along its whole length. He could feel the diamonds of it printing into her back through the silk, under his hands, and she didn't care, and behind him the candles guttered in a breath off the falls and came back. For a first kiss it had no manners at all.
He kissed her again. The first had been paid on a dare in front of the people who ran Hollis, with a jazz trio for cover.

else.text: He kissed her again. The first had been paid on top of a wall, like a debt she'd promised to settle.
Nobody had dared this one. It went slower and it cost more, with a dead girl's candles burning a few feet away, and she kissed him back like she'd decided to pay it anyway.

body.text: Gravel, under tires.

A car came down the dam road with its headlights off, slow, the moon sliding along its roof, and turned into the pull-off. Square-backed and boxy, a wagon, some dark color the moon couldn't settle on. The engine cut. It ticked as it cooled.
Del had his wrist before he'd finished turning. They went down behind the sumac by the fence on their knees in the gravel, her shoulder in his ribs, the silk hissing against the leaves.
The car door opened and no dome light came on. A man got out and shut the door with his hip, quietly, the way you shut a door in a house where somebody's asleep.

A little under six feet. Solid through the shoulders. A bottle-green blazer with brass buttons; Cal had seen thirty of them tonight and could have drawn the buttons from memory. A penlight came on in the man's hand, a small white coin of light, and he walked it to the shrine.
He read the oar blade. The light stayed on the letters a long time. Then he stood very still, the way men stand at a casket when the prayer has run out and they don't want to be seen leaving.
He hummed. Low, a few bars, barely over the water.

*The Parting Glass.* They had played it at Ricky Dolan's wake in July, a fiddle and a drunk tenor in the back room of the Quiet Man, and Cal had stood by the door the whole time. Half of Irish Boston could hum it. He didn't want to know which half this was.

The man took the blade in both hands and pulled it off the fence. He carried it to the concrete lip above the headrace, where the water ran smooth and fast toward the edge of the dam, and threw it, hard. It turned once in the moonlight, white letters up, hit the headrace and went along it faster than a man could run, and went over the Ladder. Nothing came up below.
He stood there a long time after. A stone was cutting into Cal's knee. Del's breath against his neck came in small pieces, held and let go.

Then the penlight swung. It came across the gravel and into the sumac, across the leaves an inch from Cal's face, across them, maybe, or only across the bushes they were in, and away, pointed at the ground, walking.
The door. The engine. The car backed out dark and went up the dam road all the way to the bridge, where the headlights came on at last and swept the river once and turned toward town.
They never saw his face.
Del was shaking. He could feel it through the silk, a fine fast tremor like a wire in wind.
"We weren't here," she said.

choices.label: "We were never here."
"Somebody just threw a dead girl's apology in the river, Del. Somebody should know."

then.text: "Tell them what?" She sat back on her heels in the gravel. "That Teddy Vanderhoef and a waitress named Jo saw a man throw away a sorry note?"
He heard it the way a desk sergeant would, at two in the morning, from a kid in a borrowed name and a girl with no shoes. He agreed. It cost him nothing at all, and he hated that it cost him nothing.

body.text: "We were never here," Cal said.
"Not at the party. Not at the river."
"Not anywhere."

She spat in her palm and held it out, which he'd have bet money no Ashcombe in history had ever done, and he laughed out loud, there in the bushes, and spat in his and took it. It was a joke. Her hand was wet and hot and shaking, and neither of them let go first, and they knelt there holding on long after the joke was over.

Then they ran, up the dam road with the Ladder falling away behind them, past the Ferryhouse without looking at it, up the long hill, laughing so hard they had to hang on somebody's picket fence, and nearly dying of fright when a sprinkler came on with a cough two houses up. Over the campus the Beacon started striking two. Del ran with her shoes in her hand and the paper bag in the other, and they passed the Krug back and forth until there wasn't any. Calder Falls slept through all of it.
At the Hollis gates she stood the empty bottle on the gatepost, upright, like a candle, and they went in.

Teddy's bed was made. Somebody, Bunny probably, had turned the duvet down at one corner like a hotel, and nobody had touched it since. The room smelled of new carpet and Teddy's cologne, and through the open window, from all the way down the hill, came the race: a long hiss under everything, like a radio left on in another room.

Cal's half looked like a cell somebody was about to leave on parole. The Sox pennant. The twins at Castle Island squinting over two Sully's cones. A stack of quarters by the desk lamp for the laundry, six dollars squared off like poker chips. And over his bed, Patty's crucifix, which he'd hung at noon without thinking and then couldn't take down because Teddy had watched him hang it.
There was now a girl in green silk standing under it, and Jesus was looking straight at her. Cal discovered that he had a limit on how Catholic he could be at two in the morning.
"Is he staying?" Del said.

"Not before Christmas, if he's smart. Why, you want to meet his mother?" He pulled his orientation T-shirt off the chair and draped it over the cross. It made things worse. It looked like Jesus had gone into witness protection.

then.text: The lantern sat on his desk between his Discman and a box of Cheez-Its, a hundred and seventy years of brass and soot that looked, in here, like something from a yard sale in Quincy.

body.text: Cal clicked the desk lamp off, and the room went to streetlight and a thin ghost of moon.

Del went straight to the silver mini stereo on Teddy's dresser, ejected the iPod from its dock like a woman unloading a gun, and found a burned disc in the tray, TED MIX SUMMER 05 in Sharpie. She pressed play without asking, skipped twice, and stopped.

body.text: "Teddy has taste," she said. "How disappointing. I'd built a whole picture."
Then she stood in front of the twins.

then.text: "Siobhan and Patrick," she said. Not a question.
He didn't answer. She didn't push, and he would remember that longer than she'd have guessed.

else.text: "Who're they?"
"Later."
She looked at him over her shoulder, deciding whether later was a real place. "Later," she agreed.

body.text: She unbuckled the gold watch, the little square one she'd been turning all night, and laid it face down on his desk beside the quarters. Then she turned around and stood there in the streetlight with her hands at her sides, waiting to see what he'd do with her.

choices.label: Let her lead.
Lead. She's waiting to see if you will.
Slow it down. Make her wait.

body.text: He took one step and she put a finger on his sternum and stopped him exactly where she wanted him.
"You did me up," she said, and turned and lifted her hair off her neck. "Fair's fair."

The zip went down easier than it had gone up. At twenty to eleven he'd been careful to touch her only with the zipper. Now the backs of his fingers rode her spine all the way to the small of her back, and the silk opened like a letter. She stepped out of it and left it where it fell, a puddle of green on Teddy's rug worth more than everything Cal owned. Pearls, and nothing under the dress but a strip of flesh-colored lace she took off without ceremony.

Then she undressed him like a customs officer. Teddy's tie she slid off and hung around her own neck, over the pearls, which was the most obscene thing he'd ever seen. His grandfather's blazer she put on the back of the chair, carefully, squaring the shoulders, as if she knew. Shirt. Belt. She stopped at his arms.
"You have a farmer's tan."
"Construction."
"I'll allow it."

She pushed him down onto the extra-long twin and it complained. Under the sheet the mattress was the vinyl kind, and every move they made crackled like a candy wrapper. His knuckles hit the radiator. She laughed into his mouth, then took his wrists and put them over his head against the cold iron and kept them there.

"Be loud," she said. "The walls are cinderblock, darling." Then again, lower, with her mouth against his jaw: "Be loud, *Cal*." His name came out of her stretched wide, the vowel left out in the sun, and he noticed, and he was busy.

So he was. She went down his chest with her mouth, slow, the tie trailing behind her, and took his cock in her hand, then in her mouth, watching his face the whole time like she was checking a hand of cards. He said "Jesus" and then looked at the T-shirt on the wall and said "Sorry" and she laughed around him, which nearly finished it right there.
She reached over the side of the bed for the beaded evening bag and came up with a condom.
"Grandmother's bag."
"Your grandmother carried—"

"Different era." She rolled it on him with quick, sure hands, better at it than any heiress had a right to be. It had been in that bag since before he zipped her. He decided not to ask who it had been packed for, and noticed that the deciding hurt.
She lowered herself onto him an inch at a time, her mouth open, her long thighs shaking with the control of it.

Giving her the wheel was the best thing that had ever happened to him. She rode him like she was steering something through weather, and when she looked down at him too long he put his forearm over his eyes, because being looked at was worse than being naked.

Then he forgot himself and sat up to get his hands on her, to roll her under him, and her palm came down flat on his chest and pushed him back into the vinyl. For half a second her face wasn't playing at all.
He lay back. He kept his hands where she'd put them. That was the truest thing he did all night, and he didn't say a word about it.

He crossed the room in three steps and took her face in both hands and kissed her like he'd been sent to collect a debt. She made a small surprised sound against his mouth, and her hands went to his shirt and stayed there, waiting to see.

He turned her around himself. The zip he'd done up at twenty to eleven came down one long stroke, and he followed it with his mouth, the knobs of her spine, the warm salt of her back, all the way down until he was on his knees on Teddy's rug and the green silk slid over his shoulders and pooled around her feet.
"Somebody's been practicing," she said to the window.
"Big parish."

He was good, and he knew he was good, and some part of him was standing in the corner of 304 with its arms folded, grading. He got her pearls off one-handed. He lifted her and carried her the four feet to the bed like a fireman, which was a show, and the show ended when his elbow cracked into the radiator and he said "Mother of God" and dropped her the last six inches onto a mattress that squeaked like a bag of chips.
She lay there laughing at him with her whole long body. "Is this what Teddy would do?"
"Teddy would ask permission in Latin."
"So ask."
"Can I—"
"Yes. Christ. *Yes*, Reardon, keep up."

He put his mouth between her legs and went at it like an audition, and she let him for maybe a minute before she took his chin and lifted his head and said, quite kindly, "Stop performing. Nobody's grading you."

So he stopped. He slowed down and listened to her, which turned out to be a different thing from showing her, and she told him things without words: where, and harder, and there, *there*, her heel digging into his back, the dancer's line of her thigh going tight under his hand. Somewhere in it she stopped narrating. For a girl who had talked all night, the quiet was the loudest thing she'd done. When she came she did it with both hands over her mouth, which was the first thing she'd hidden from him on purpose since the closet.
She found the beaded evening bag on the floor without looking and fished out a condom.
"Grandmother's bag."
"Your grandmother carried—"
"Different era." She tore it open with her teeth. It had been in the bag since before he zipped her. He decided not to ask who it was packed for, and noticed that the deciding hurt. "Come here."
He came up her body and she rolled it onto him herself, and he went into her slowly, propped on his forearms. Streetlight from the window lay across her. He looked at her too long.
"Don't stare," she said, in a voice she'd borrowed from somebody's grandmother. "It's common."
He laughed into her neck, because he could hear that it was borrowed and that she wanted him to hear it, and she held on to him like the bed was moving.
She reached for him and he caught her wrists.
"No."
Her eyebrow went up, the one from the Bramwell steps. "No?"
"Not no. Not yet."

She'd been daring him all night, down a cellar and over a wall. Going faster was the only direction either of them knew. He turned her around and found the tab of the zip and drew it down one tooth at a time.
"You're joking."
"I did this up in about eleven seconds. I'm getting my money's worth."

He kissed the back of her neck and moved the zip a quarter inch. He kissed the top of her spine and moved it again. By the time it reached the small of her back she was swearing at him in a register he'd never heard out of anyone in pearls. The green silk went down onto Teddy's rug, and she stepped out of it and turned around in a temper and he held her wrists again.
"You bastard," she said. "You absolute Boston bastard."
"Hands at your sides."
She put them there, which surprised them both.

He undressed himself without hurrying, the blazer on the chair, Teddy's tie on the floor, her eyes going over his chest and his arms and the line of his tan with an expression she hadn't decided on yet. He walked her back until her calves hit the bed. The mattress was vinyl under the sheet and squeaked when she sat. She lay back on it with her long legs bent, a bar of streetlight across her stomach, breathing like she'd run up the hill again.
He took the pearls off like it was delicate surgery, which it wasn't, it was one clasp, and he made such a production of it that she laughed and called him an idiot.

"Put those somewhere safe," she said, and she wasn't joking, and he heard it. He laid them on the desk beside the watch like something that might need a priest, and when he came back she took his face in her hand as if to check it was the same boy. Then she stopped looking and he put his mouth to her breast. He used his fingers slowly, inside her, her wet heat around them, and when she pushed her hips up for more he took them away and kissed the inside of her knee instead.
"I will kill you," she said. "I'll have you killed. I know people."
"You know caterers."
"*Reardon*."

He gave her back his hand and took it away again, twice, until she was arching off the bed and the radiator rattled where her foot kicked it. She was undone and furious about it and plainly loving it, her laugh coming out of her in pieces. She groped over the edge of the bed for the beaded evening bag and threw a condom at his face.
"Grandmother's bag."
"Your grandmother carried—"
"Different era. Hurry the hell up."

He caught it. It had been in the bag since before he zipped her, and he decided not to ask who it was packed for, and noticed that the deciding hurt. He didn't hurry. He rolled it on and went into her slowly enough that she said every word she knew, and some, he was fairly sure, she had made up for the occasion.

then.text: She had slowed to a long, deliberate roll of her hips, sitting up on him with Teddy's tie still around her neck, the window behind her. She leaned down and he thought she was going to kiss him.
He was over her, moving slow, and she had stopped hiding her face. She looked up at him in the streetlight like she was reading small print.
He was moving in her at the pace he'd set, and it was killing her, and she'd stopped pretending it wasn't. She looked up at him with her hair stuck to her cheek and her eyes narrow.

body.text: She put her thumb on the scar through his eyebrow. Lightly, the way you test paint.
"Hockey," he said.
"Liar."
"Takes one."
He'd told Teddy it was a bar fight. Tomorrow he'd tell somebody it was a church raffle. It was the one story he never told the same way twice.
She stopped moving. She did it on purpose, the way you'd put a hand down flat on a table.

then.text: She sat all the way down on him and stayed there, perfectly still, her palms on his chest, and he made a noise he'd be ashamed of later.
She took a fistful of his hair and made him look up, and held him there, deep inside her, and she was stronger in that position than he was, and they both knew it.
She locked her legs around him and held him still and said nothing at all. She just looked at him, which was worse.

body.text: "Rule two," she said. "You got caught. You owe me one true thing."
The stereo had moved on to something he didn't know. She waited, holding him, like a woman with all the leverage in the world.

then.text: "The picture," he said. "On the wall."
She didn't look at it. She looked at him.

"Siobhan and Patrick. They're twelve. Twins. Shiv's older by eleven minutes and she brings it up." He was talking too fast and couldn't slow down. "Gold Street, third floor. My mother works nights, so I did mornings. Lunches. Shiv's permission slips, she forges them better than I do. Sister Margaret at the school has my number, not my mother's. Pat can't sleep when the radiator bangs and it bangs all winter, so I'd sit up with him and we'd watch old Bruins tapes because there were no Bruins, the lockout, the whole winter, and—" He lost the end of the sentence and went looking for it. "And yesterday I got on a bus. I left them a note on the fridge, basically."
Neither of them moved.
"Anyway," he said. "Shiv'll have the rent figured out by Tuesday."
It came out like a bag splitting. He'd said better things to girls about nothing.

Del went very quiet. Her hand moved from the scar to the side of his face and stayed there, gentle in a way he hadn't seen from her yet, all the jokes gone out of her. Her thumb stopped on his cheek and didn't know where to go.
"Okay," she said, so softly it barely counted as a word. "Okay. That's paid."
She kissed the scar. Then she started to move again, slow, holding on to him like he was the one who needed holding.
"I wanted you since the eyebrow," he said.
"Which eyebrow?"
"You know which eyebrow. Bramwell steps. You, a trunk the size of a Buick, and that eyebrow, like I'd tracked mud in."
She considered it with her thumb still on his scar. "That's the cheap one."
"It's true."

"It's true *and* it's cheap. You've got a whole wallet in there and you paid me out of the change jar." The corner of her mouth went up. She was enjoying this more than the real thing would have let her. "Fine. I'll take it. I'm keeping the change."
She unlocked her hold on him by degrees, like she was letting out a line.
"Run me a tab," he said.
"A *tab*."
"I'm good for it."
She looked down at him, or up, flushed, holding him still, and something in her face went soft around the edges, like a bill folded and unfolded too many times.
"You'd better be."
"I'm from Southie. We're good for everything. Eventually."

"Then I'll hold your paper, Reardon." She said it like a promise and a threat at once, and she liked it, he could tell. She liked having something of his in her pocket. She let him go an inch at a time.

body.text: After that neither of them was funny for a while.

then.text: She rode him hard now, her hands braced on the wall over his head where the crucifix hid under the T-shirt, the bed knocking the radiator in time.
He moved in her harder now and she met him, her nails in his back, the bed knocking the radiator in time.
He stopped making her wait. She dragged him down to her by Teddy's discarded tie, which she'd found somewhere on the floor, and the bed knocked the radiator in time.

body.text: The vinyl shouted every move to the hall. Sweat ran between them and the sheet came off the corner of the mattress and nobody fixed it. She was loud, and then louder, unembarrassed, telling him yes and don't stop and *Cal*, and he told her what she felt like, badly, in pieces. Like a snow day. Like the whole city shutting down for you. "That's the worst thing anyone's ever said to me," she panted. "Don't stop." When she came it went through her from her heels up, and her voice dropped out of the one she'd worn all night.
"*Lord*," she said. Long and low, the vowel taking its time, two syllables where the voice she'd arrived in would have allowed one.
It went in under everything else and he kept it. He put it on the shelf with the supper and the stacked plates.
He was close, and he said her name. "Del."

She flinched. Barely, a flinch you'd only feel from inside, her whole body hitching once like she'd heard it called across a parking lot. Then she pulled him in by the back of the neck and held him through it, and he came with his face in her hair, her heels locked behind him, saying nothing at all.

Afterward they lay on the narrow bed, tangled because there was no other way to fit, her head on his chest and his foot against the radiator. The window was a square of hazy streetlight. Down the hill the race kept up its hiss. The sweat cooled on them in the heat that wasn't cooling at all. Over the Commons the Beacon gave a quarter-hour, he couldn't have said of what. Teddy's disc ran out, and the stereo clicked once and went silent, and the room was just the two of them breathing.

Promise nothing. Let her think you're asleep.

then.text: "Tomorrow night," he said into her hair. "Same bed. I'll even make it."
She laughed against his chest. "We were never here, Teddy. You can't have a second night of never."
But she didn't say no. Her foot found his ankle under the twisted sheet and hooked it, and stayed.
"Where'd the 'Lord' come from?"
She didn't miss a step. "Honestly, Reardon, Grandmother's cook was from Savannah. I spent every summer in her kitchen, shelling things. One picks it up."
It was a very good answer. It was the kind of answer he'd have given.

Her right hand went to her left wrist to turn the watch. Her fingers closed on bare skin, and she let them rest there a moment as if that had been the plan, and then she put the hand flat on his stomach. He saw the reach. He didn't say anything about it.
He said nothing. He shut his eyes and let his breathing go long and slow, the way he used to for Pat, until it was almost true.

Her breathing changed. She'd decided he was asleep. After a while she said something to the ceiling, very low, too quiet for him to make out a single word. It wasn't meant for him. He didn't try to hear it.

body.text: She fell asleep first. It seemed to surprise her: she jerked once, like someone missing a step on a staircase, and then she was gone, heavy and warm across him. Or she was pretending. With her he couldn't have sworn to either.
He woke alone, on his back, with the sheet in a rope around one leg and the window gone the gray of dishwater.

The green silk was gone off Teddy's rug. The watch was gone from the desk. His gray hoodie was gone from the back of the chair, the one with SOUTH BOSTON across the chest and a hole in the cuff where his thumb went through. And the quarters were gone, the whole stack, six dollars of laundry. A girl with a Krug habit and a watch like that, walking out at dawn with a fistful of laundry money. He'd have understood the hoodie. He didn't understand the quarters at all.
The desk lamp was on. It burned yellow and pointless in the daylight.

Somewhere after the window went gray he'd surfaced far enough to hear the stairwell door at the end of the hall let out its long pneumatic sigh. Then, a while later, again. He had turned over into the warm place she'd left and gone back down both times.
On the pillow beside his head was a photograph.

body.caption: We were never here. — D.
body.text: Cal asleep, one arm over his face, lamp-lit.

He turned it over. The writing on the back was careful and upright, every letter finished before the next one started, like something copied out of a book by somebody determined not to make a mistake. He'd seen a hand like that somewhere, recently. The thought got as far as the edge of waking and went back under.

then.text: He had promised her tomorrow night. She had left him a photograph.
He turned over the Savannah cook, and the bare wrist, and found he liked neither answer better than the other.
He wondered what she'd said to the ceiling.
He had told her about the twins. He lay there and tried to be sorry and couldn't get it to take.
He still owed her one true thing. She had taken six dollars on account.
On the desk the founders' lantern stood where he'd left it. On its glass chimney, low on one side, was a print of her mouth in the soot, clean as a stamp.

body.text: The door opened at a quarter to seven and Teddy came in sideways, in last night's shirt, carrying his loafers.

He smelled of a cologne that wasn't his, something with smoke in it. His hair had been slept on, but not in a bed. He looked rumpled and a little high on something he wasn't going to share, and for once he didn't look scared of anything.
"Reardon," he said. "How was I?"
"You were magnificent."

then.text: *Northampton*, Cal thought, and let him have it.

body.text: Teddy grinned at the ceiling like the answer was a gift. "I knew it. I *knew* I had it in me."

then.text: Then he saw the desk and stopped. He put both hands on top of his head.
"Wait, wait, wait. Is that the— Reardon. That's—okay, that's actually amazing."
He circled it like it might go off, and laughed once, high and helpless. "My father will put it in the Christmas letter. He'll say I 'took an interest in the club's heritage.'"

body.text: On his way back to the door for his shower caddy he stepped on something, and it crinkled under his foot. A plain white envelope, slid under the door while the room slept. He picked it up. Typed capitals:
**THEODORE VANDERHOEF IV — 304**
Teddy read it twice and flicked it across the room. It hit Cal in the chest.
"You got mail, Theodore." He slung a towel around his neck. "I'm going to shower. I smell like a decision."
The door shut behind him. The envelope wasn't sealed. Inside was a glossy print, four by six, the drugstore kind.

It was him. Cal Reardon in Teddy's tie on the Corinthian terrace, laughing at something with his whole face, a hurricane lantern burning behind his ear. At the edge of the frame was a tweed shoulder, and nobody but Sloane had worn tweed in August. Out of focus over Cal's other shoulder, turned half away, was a blonde in green silk.
Behind the photograph was a white index card. Typed, same machine:
*You weren't at the dam last night. Neither was I. —*

Cal stood up with the card in one hand and went to the window. The air coming in was already hot. Below him the roofs of Calder Falls went down the hill in the haze, past the steeple of St. Anne's and the dead brick mill, to the granite cube of the Ferryhouse on its bluff. Beyond it the river lay flat and pale, and at the Ladder it went over in one long white line.
